design_detail: Mixed-methods analysis nested in an open-label, single-arm study of psilocybin with psychological support for treatment-resistant depression at Imperial College London. 19 patients each received oral psilocybin 10 mg and, one week later, 25 mg (study conditions), lying with eye-shades in a furnished room with two therapists while one standardized playlist played from ingestion (one patient who strongly disliked it in the first session heard a different playlist in the second). One week after the 25 mg session each patient gave a semi-structured interview about the music in both sessions. Qualitative part: interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) with counts of how many patients mentioned each theme. Quantitative part: four researchers blind to identity and outcome rated each transcript for music liking, resonance and openness; the averaged ratings were correlated (Pearson, n = 19) with the percentage fall in QIDS-SR16 depression scores recorded at the same one-week time point (the paper does not say it was the same visit), with five principal components of the 11-dimension Altered States of Consciousness scale (11D-ASC), and with a self-rated drug-intensity scale. No control condition; music was never varied or withheld.
can_establish: What these 19 patients said the music did during their psilocybin sessions (welcome and unwelcome influences, with counts), and that patients whose one-week interviews described the music more favourably also reported larger falls in depression scores at that time point and higher scores on an ASC-derived mystical-experience factor.
cannot_establish: That music, or a liked or resonant music experience, caused better outcomes or more mystical experiences (no control condition, music not varied, no adjustment, predictor recorded at the same time point as the outcome and after the acute-experience ratings), that music mediates outcomes (no mediation analysis), or how far the findings apply beyond a small, highly selected trial sample.

sample.recruitment: Patients of the Imperial College London open-label study of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016a, as cited; Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 1st paragraph). How patients were recruited is not described in this paper.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: moderate to severe major depression (21-item HAM-D score of 17 or more) with no improvement despite at least two different antidepressant treatments of at least 6 weeks within the current episode. Excluded: current or previous psychotic disorder, psychotic disorder in an immediate family member, suicide attempt requiring hospitalisation, mania, blood or needle phobia, pregnancy, current drug or alcohol dependence (Methods › Participants).
sample.demographics: Not reported in this paper: age, sex, baseline depression scores and medication status are referred to the parent trial report.
sample.attrition: All 19 patients were interviewed and completed the QIDS at baseline and one week after the 25 mg session (Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 4th paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph). The paper does not say whether any patient of the parent study was not interviewed.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers with treatment-resistant depression who entered a psilocybin trial (expectations not measured), treated in a hospital research facility with two therapists and a 4-hour preparation visit that included listening to samples of the session music. The analysed sample equals the interviewed sample; whether it equals the whole trial cohort is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Music experience: three 0–100 visual analogue ratings (liking, resonance, openness; five verbal anchors each), made independently by four researchers blind to patient identifiers and treatment outcomes, from transcripts of interviews held one week after the 25 mg session that covered both sessions; the four raters' scores were averaged per patient (Methods › Ratings for music experience, 2nd paragraph; Correlation analyses, 1st paragraph). The three variables were chosen because they showed a notable polarity in the same transcripts during coding and were then hypothesised as predictors (Methods › Ratings for music experience, 1st paragraph). Drug intensity: the patient's own 0–100 rating of peak drug effects, made after each session (Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: synthetic psilocybin (THC-Pharm) formulated into 5 mg capsules, taken by mouth, 10 mg in the first session and 25 mg one week later, by every patient (open label); dosing at 10.30 am after arrival at 9 am, most patients ready to leave about 7 hours after dosing (Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). Music: one standardized playlist (mainly contemporary ambient, neo-classical, contemporary classical and traditional or ethnic styles, chosen to limit religious associations), arranged by phases (pre-onset, ascent, peak, descent, return), with the most emotionally evocative pieces at the peak, started at ingestion and played through in-ear headphones and a hi-fi speaker carrying the same signal. One patient who strongly disliked the music in the first session received a different playlist (used at Johns Hopkins University) in the second (Methods › Therapeutic setting; Music selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Playlist design). The full playlist is in the online supplement, which was not opened.
exposure.polysubstance: Current drug or alcohol dependence excluded. Other drug use, and antidepressant or other medication at the time of the sessions, are not reported in this paper.

comparison.controls: None. Single-arm, open-label study: every patient received psilocybin with music; there was no placebo, no music-free condition and no alternative-music arm. The quantitative analysis compares patients who described the music more or less favourably.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Nothing was measured before the sessions about music preferences, personality (for example openness or absorption), expectancy or the relationship with the therapists; baseline depression severity is not reported here and was not used as a covariate.

outcomes.instruments: 16-item Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptoms, self-rated (QIDS-SR16), at screening and one week after the 25 mg session, expressed as percentage reduction from baseline; 11D-ASC completed at the end of the session, reduced by principal component analysis with varimax rotation to five components labelled mystical experience, impaired cognition, audiovisual perception, anxiety and insightfulness; drug-intensity visual analogue scale; semi-structured interview with four open questions about how the music influenced the experience, analysed by IPA (Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 1st and 4th paragraphs; The semi-structured interview; Correlation analyses, 1st paragraph; Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: QIDS and the ASC are established self-report scales. The liking, resonance and openness ratings were made up for this study from interview transcripts; agreement between the four raters averaged r = 0.6 (± 0.1, not stated to be an SD) over 18 rater-pair correlations, which the authors call good, and the three ratings correlated r = 0.90 to 0.96 with each other, which the authors read as probably one construct. Mystical experience was not measured with the Mystical Experience Questionnaire; the term labels a component loaded by three ASC dimensions (experience of unity, spiritual experience, blissful state) (footnote 1).
outcomes.operationalization: Clinical improvement: percentage fall in QIDS score from screening to one week after the 25 mg session. A good music experience: high averaged ratings of liking, resonance and openness from the one-week interview. Prediction: a bivariate Pearson correlation in 19 patients, not a model with covariates.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: False discovery rate control (Benjamini–Hochberg) across the correlations, with an adjusted significance threshold stated as p = 0.016 (Results › Predictors…, 2nd paragraph). Two printed p values do not fit their r values at n = 19 (see reporting issues), and one of them bears on whether a result passes that threshold.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The four music-experience raters were blind to patient identifiers and outcomes, but they rated transcripts recorded at the same time point as the outcome questionnaire, in which patients could describe how they were doing. Depression and ASC scores were self-rated by patients who knew they had received psilocybin (open label).

analysis.effect_sizes: Pearson r, n = 19 (Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph). Percentage fall in QIDS at one week: liking r = 0.60 (p = .006), resonance r = 0.59 (p = .008), openness r = 0.57 (printed p = .001), drug intensity r = 0.004 (p = 0.98). Editors' calculation (Fisher z, n = 19), 95% intervals: liking 0.20 to 0.83, resonance 0.19 to 0.82, openness 0.16 to 0.81, drug intensity -0.45 to 0.46. Mystical-experience component: liking r = 0.61 (p = .006), resonance r = 0.67 (p = .002), openness r = 0.70 (p = .0008), drug intensity r = 0.58 (p = 0.009). Insightfulness component: resonance r = 0.53 (printed p = .016), openness r = 0.59 (p = .007), drug intensity r = 0.65 (p = 0.002), liking r = 0.44 (p = .06). Impaired cognition (r = 0.55, p = 0.01) and audiovisual perception (r = 0.71, p = 0.0006) correlated with drug intensity and with none of the music variables; the anxiety component correlated with none. The music variables correlated with each other at r = 0.9, 0.96 and 0.91 and, by the text, not with drug intensity (values not printed) (Results › Inter-rating reliability and discriminative validity of music experience variables). Correlations that were not significant appear only in Figure 4, an image that was not viewable in this reading; their values were not extracted.
analysis.covariates: None: bivariate correlations only. Baseline depression severity, the overall quality of the acute experience and expectancy were not adjusted for.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration, protocol or analysis plan is cited in this paper. The three music predictors were derived from the coding of the same interviews and then hypothesised as predictors (Methods › Ratings for music experience, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Correlations that were not significant are not given as numbers in the text (only in the Figure 4 image), including those of the music variables with the anxiety, impaired-cognition and audiovisual components and with drug intensity. The Introduction hypothesizes that music promotes mystical experiences, which in turn predict outcome, but the correlation of the mystical-experience component with the fall in depression is not reported, so that pathway was not tested in the paper.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation. With n = 19 the 95% interval for r = 0.60 runs from about 0.20 to 0.83 (editors' calculation). Whether the music correlations differ from the drug-intensity correlation was not tested formally; the abstract contrasts a significant with a non-significant correlation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 19 patients of an open-label trial, more favourable descriptions of the music, rated from interviews held at the one-week visit, went with larger falls in self-rated depression at that same one-week time point (r about 0.6, with wide intervals) and with higher mystical-experience and insightfulness component scores from questionnaires completed at the end of the session; self-rated drug intensity did not correlate with the change in depression. In the interviews, 18 of 19 patients described welcome and 10 of 19 unwelcome influences of the music.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the nature of the music experience significantly predictive of reductions in depression, unlike drug intensity, and concludes that music plays a central therapeutic function (Abstract). The Discussion says the findings indicate that an interaction between drug and music promotes positive outcomes (Discussion › Music experience predicts experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph) and that outcomes “suffered” when the music was dissonant, disliked or resisted (Discussion › Implications for the use of music in psychedelic therapy, 1st paragraph); the Conclusions speak of a central mediating role for music. No mediation was tested, music was never varied or withheld, nothing was adjusted, and the predictor was recorded at the same time point as the outcome and a week after the ASC ratings it is said to predict, so patients who had improved may have recalled and described the music more warmly. The Limitations concede that, without a placebo condition, causal inference is problematic and that the data were mainly qualitative (Limitations and future directions, 1st paragraph).

timeline.event: Parent study: open-label feasibility study of psilocybin with psychological support for treatment-resistant depression (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016a, as cited for the clinical outcomes; not read for this card).

Correction (10.1007/s00213-018-4886-8, Psychopharmacology 235:1623, read): the article became open access under a CC BY 4.0 licence on 19 March 2018, and the co-author listed as Christopher Timmerman should be Christopher Timmermann. No data or conclusions changed.

Strickland et al. (2021): randomized comparison of musical genres in psilocybin sessions, named in the project's BeforeDuring evidence map as the one randomized comparison of music (not read for this card).

Nader (2025), opinion article written in response to this paper (10.3389/fpsyt.2025.1652568, read for this card): argues that music may act as a confounder that displaces the patient's own psychological material, states that no controlled research compares music with silent settings and calls for randomized comparisons; it also raises a possible conflict of interest of the first author as head of a company providing music for psychedelic therapy. No new data.

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication of the correlation is listed in the project's evidence map (2026-10-31). Whether music, or a particular kind of music experience, changes the outcome of psychedelic therapy has not been tested by randomizing music against silence; Nader (2025) states that no controlled research makes that comparison.

funding.funder: No funding section in the article. The conflict-of-interest statement names the Beckley Foundation as one of the sponsors of the study. The Methods state that Imperial College London's Joint Research and Compliance Office sponsored and approved the study, that the National Institute for Health Research Clinical Research Network adopted it, and that the NIHR/Wellcome Trust Imperial Clinical Research Facility approved the site (Methods › Approvals; Compliance with ethical standards).
funding.declared_conflicts: Amanda Feilding is the director of the Beckley Foundation, one of the sponsors of the study; David Nutt is an advisor for the Beckley Foundation (Compliance with ethical standards › Conflict of interest). No other interests declared.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Psychedelic Research Group and C3NL at Imperial College London, the School of Psychology at Sussex University, and the Beckley Foundation. The first author's earlier studies of LSD and music are cited in the Introduction. The paper does not say who designed the playlist, who conducted the interviews or who coded them. Nader (2025) states that the first author is CEO of a company providing music for psychedelic therapy; the 2018 paper declares no such interest, and Nader does not date the role. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized comparison within a psilocybin trial of music against silence (and of a fixed playlist against one adapted to the patient), with the music experience rated on the session day before any outcome is known, outcome raters blind to condition, adjustment for baseline severity and for the intensity and quality of the acute experience, a pre-registered analysis plan and follow-up beyond one week.

domains.note: No adjustment. The music ratings correlate strongly with the mystical-experience component (r 0.61 to 0.70); a generally good or bad session, expectancy, the relationship with the therapists or baseline severity could drive both how the music is remembered and how mood changes, and the paper itself cites its group's report that the quality of the acute experience predicts outcome (Roseman et al., 2017). Drug intensity, one self-rated item, is the only alternative examined, and only in separate bivariate correlations.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: The exposure was rated from interviews held one week after the 25 mg session, at the same time point as the outcome questionnaire and after any improvement had happened, so current mood and outcome can shape how the music is recalled and described. The three ratings were derived from the same transcripts, are not validated and agreed only moderately between raters (average r 0.6). Raters were blind to outcome, but the transcripts could reveal how patients were doing.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study (or into the analysis)
domains.note: All 19 interviewed patients were analysed, but the paper does not say whether the parent study enrolled others who were not interviewed; a small, highly selected volunteer sample.

The playlist was changed for one patient after strong dislike in the first session, and the therapists checked in every 30 to 60 minutes and could give psychological support depending on how the session was going; these responses are neither described per patient nor analysed.
QIDS completed by all 19 at both time points; every transcript rated by all four raters.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: QIDS is self-rated in an open-label study by the same patients whose interview supplied the exposure, at the same time point, which invites a common-method correlation; the outcome is only one week after the last session.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registered analysis plan; predictors chosen from the qualitative coding; principal component analysis of 11 ASC scales in 19 patients; non-significant correlations shown only in a figure; the hypothesized link between mystical experience and outcome not reported; two printed p values do not match their r values.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Mixed-methods study: the quantitative part (correlations of the music experience with outcome) is appraised with ROBINS-E as the round's brief asks, and the qualitative part is described, not rated. Its qualitative method has strengths (independent coding by at least two researchers, an interview guide printed in full, theme counts across all patients) and limits (one interviewer for 18 of 19 interviews, no reflexive account of the team's stake in music, no saturation account, quotations held in a supplement that was not read). Two ROBINS-E domains are high, and each could by itself produce the reported association: confounding by the overall quality of the session, and an exposure recorded after, and alongside, the outcome. ROBINS-E rates the result very high when several domains are high in ways that substantially lower confidence. The card may be cited for what these 19 patients said the music did (welcome and unwelcome influences, with counts) and for the correlations as a hypothesis, stated with their intervals and the timing of measurement. It should not be cited as showing that music, or a liked or resonant music experience, improves the outcome of psilocybin therapy, or that music mediates its effects.

key_findings.finding: Design facts: 19 patients with treatment-resistant depression, open label, oral psilocybin 10 mg then 25 mg one week apart (study conditions); QIDS at screening and one week after the 25 mg session; 11D-ASC at the end of the session; drug-intensity rating after each session; music interview one week after the 25 mg session, covering both sessions.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants; Experiment overview and procedures, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; The semi-structured interview, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Interviews (mean 1,048 words, SE 133) yielded four groups of themes: welcome influences of the music in 18 of 19 patients (95%), unwelcome influences in 10 of 19 (53%), appreciated music styles or playlist features in all 19, and unappreciated styles or features in 11 of 19 (58%).

Welcome influences: intensification of the experience in 17 of 19 (of emotion 15 of 17, of imagery 9 of 17, general 8 of 17); guidance in 15 of 19 (a sense of being on a journey 11 of 15, support 11 of 15, music matching the emotional state 6 of 15, continuity and direction 5 of 15); calming in 10 of 19; openness to the music-evoked experience in 7 of 19, of whom 6 described being open to challenging experience as important and therapeutic.
key_findings.locator: Results › Welcome influences: intensification, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Welcome influences of the music: guidance, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Welcome influence of the music: calming; Welcome influences of the music: openness to music-evoked experience

key_findings.finding: Unwelcome influences: music intensifying emotions patients did not want, such as fear or sadness (5 of the 10 with unwelcome influences), discomfort (5 of 10) and irritation (4 of 10); resistance to the music-evoked experience in 9 of 19 (47%); a sense of misguidance in 6 of 19 (32%), mostly music felt as dissonant with the unfolding experience (4 of 6).
key_findings.locator: Results › Unwelcome influences of the music: intensification; resistance to music-evoked experience; misguidance

key_findings.finding: Music styles and playlist: all 19 named styles they appreciated (ethnic styles 8 of 19; voices without lyrics or with foreign-language lyrics 7 of 19; neo-classical or classical 7 of 19); 17 of 19 appreciated the playlist design (selection 12 of 17, ordering matched to drug effects 9 of 17, the mere presence of music 6 of 17). 11 of 19 disliked some styles, with no single theme above 30%; 6 of 19 disliked aspects of the playlist design, 2 of them preferring their own music.
key_findings.locator: Results › Appreciated music styles and playlist features: music styles; playlist design; Unappreciated music styles and playlist features: music styles; playlist design

key_findings.finding: Percentage fall in QIDS at one week correlated with interview-rated music liking (r = 0.60, p = .006), resonance (r = 0.59, p = .008) and openness (r = 0.57, printed p = .001), but not with self-rated drug intensity (r = 0.004, p = 0.98); n = 19. Editors' calculation (Fisher z), 95% intervals: 0.20 to 0.83, 0.19 to 0.82, 0.16 to 0.81 and -0.45 to 0.46.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The printed p = .001 for openness does not fit r = 0.57 with n = 19 (about .011 by the editors' calculation); see reporting issues. The music ratings come from interviews at the same time point as the QIDS outcome (one week after the 25 mg session).

key_findings.finding: The mystical-experience component of the ASC correlated with music liking (r = 0.61), resonance (r = 0.67), openness (r = 0.70) and drug intensity (r = 0.58); insightfulness with resonance (r = 0.53), openness (r = 0.59) and drug intensity (r = 0.65) but not liking (r = 0.44, p = .06); impaired cognition (r = 0.55) and audiovisual perception (r = 0.71) only with drug intensity; the anxiety component with none of the variables. FDR-adjusted significance threshold stated as 0.016.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Figure 4 legend
key_findings.note: The resonance–insightfulness correlation (printed p = .016) gives about p = .020 at n = 19 (editors' calculation), above the stated threshold. The ASC was completed at the end of the session and the music ratings a week later, so the music variable cannot have been measured first.

key_findings.finding: The four raters' agreement on the music ratings averaged r = 0.6 (± 0.1, not stated to be an SD) over 18 correlations, which the authors call good; the three music ratings correlated r = 0.9, 0.96 and 0.91 with each other, and the authors note they probably represent one construct; self-rated drug intensity correlated with none of the three (values not printed).
key_findings.locator: Results › Inter-rating reliability and discriminative validity of music experience variables; Discussion › Music experience predicts experience and therapy outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state as limitations that there was no placebo condition, which makes causal inference problematic, and that the data were mainly qualitative, so the magnitude of the themes could not be studied; they present the study as giving the patients' perspective and as generating hypotheses.

Sessions took place in a furnished therapy room in a clinical research facility (medical equipment removed or hidden, adjusted lighting, cushions, plants, art); patients lay on a bed with eye-shades, two therapists checked in about every 30 to 60 minutes, and a preparation visit of about 4 hours included listening to samples of the session music with eye-shades on.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Therapeutic setting; Experiment overview and procedures, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The fall in depression correlates with openness at r = 0.57 with a printed p = .001, while the larger correlations with liking (r = 0.60) and resonance (r = 0.59) have p = .006 and .008. With the same n = 19, r = 0.57 corresponds to p of about .011 (editors' calculation, t with 17 df).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed value overstates the strength of the openness result; at about .011 it would still pass the stated FDR threshold of 0.016, so the conclusion is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: Resonance correlates with insightfulness at r = 0.53 with a printed p = .016, equal to the stated FDR threshold; with n = 19, r = 0.53 corresponds to p of about .020 (about .018 even at r = 0.535) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: By the paper's own threshold this association may not be significant; the statement that resonance predicts insightfulness is weaker than written.

reporting_issues.issue: The percentage reduction in QIDS is defined as ((baseline − post-treatment) / baseline) multiplied by −100, which makes an improvement negative; with the positive correlations reported, this formula would mean that a better music experience went with less improvement, the opposite of the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a sign slip in the formula; the direction of the main result has to be taken from the text, since Figure 4 could not be viewed.

reporting_issues.issue: Significance is described in two ways: the text gives an FDR-adjusted threshold of 0.016, while the Figure 4 legend marks p < 0.05 and p < 0.001 after FDR correction.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Predictors…, 2nd paragraph; Figure 4 legend)
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot tell which threshold each marked correlation passed.

reporting_issues.issue: The ASC was completed at the end of the session and drug intensity after each session, but the paper does not say which session's scores entered the correlations, whereas the music ratings refer to both sessions together.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 4th paragraph; The semi-structured interview)
reporting_issues.consequence: The correlations may pair measures from different sessions; the time order of exposure and outcome is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor slips: the Figure 3 legend calls the ASC dimensions acoustic features; in the unwelcome intensification cluster the percentages are labelled as of the cluster but use the 10 patients with any unwelcome influence as denominator; the resistance section refers to Table 6 as listing the themes of the cluster intensification.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Figure 3 legend; Results › Unwelcome influences of the music: intensification; resistance to music-evoked experience)
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the main findings; the size of the unwelcome intensification cluster is not stated.
